summary: How the neural tube forms and closes in week 4, how its vesicles become the adult brain and ventricles, and which cells come from neuroectoderm, neural crest, or mesoderm. Exam questions link each step to the defect that follows when it fails: neural tube defects, holoprosencephaly, and the posterior fossa malformations.

points: The notochord (mesoderm) signals the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate in week 3 (BMP4 signaling is blocked by noggin and chordin).
The edges of the plate rise as neural folds, with the neural groove between them.
The folds meet and fuse in the midline starting near the future neck in week 4, then zip toward both ends.
The open ends are the neuropores: the anterior (cranial) neuropore closes about day 25, the posterior (caudal) neuropore about day 28.
Neural crest cells peel off the crests of the folds as they fuse and migrate widely.
The notochord later persists only as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.
Three primary vesicles form by week 4: prosencephalon, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon.
By week 5 the prosencephalon splits into telencephalon and diencephalon, and the rhombencephalon into metencephalon and myelencephalon (five secondary vesicles).
The lumen of the tube becomes the ventricles, and the caudal tube becomes the spinal cord with its central canal.
The retina grows out of the diencephalon as the optic vesicle, so it is CNS tissue.
Neuroectoderm (the tube itself): CNS neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependymal cells, retina, posterior pituitary, pineal gland.
Neural crest: dorsal root and cranial sensory ganglia, autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla chromaffin cells, melanocytes.
Mesoderm: microglia (from the monocyte and macrophage line).
Spina bifida occulta: the vertebral arches fail to fuse but the cord and meninges stay inside; often a tuft of hair or dimple over the low back.
Meningocele: meninges bulge through the bony defect in a sac; the cord stays in place.
Myelomeningocele: meninges plus spinal cord or roots sit in the sac; causes leg weakness and bladder and bowel dysfunction.
Anencephaly: the anterior neuropore fails to close, so the forebrain and skull vault do not form; polyhydramnios because the fetus cannot swallow.
Open defects leak alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), raising maternal serum and amniotic fluid AFP; amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase is also high.
Skin-covered defects such as spina bifida occulta leave AFP normal.
Risk factors: low folate around conception, valproate, maternal diabetes. Folic acid 0.4 mg daily for all, 4 mg daily after a prior affected pregnancy.
The prosencephalon fails to divide into two hemispheres in weeks 5 to 6.
Linked to sonic hedgehog (SHH) pathway defects, trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), and fetal alcohol exposure.
Face and forebrain share midline signals, so the face shows midline defects: cyclopia, closely set eyes, cleft lip and palate, single central incisor.
Chiari I: cerebellar tonsils sit below the foramen magnum (usually more than 5 mm); often found in teens or adults with occipital headache worse on coughing.
Chiari I is strongly linked to a cervical syrinx (syringomyelia).
Chiari II: the cerebellar vermis and medulla herniate through the foramen magnum, with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele and obstructive hydrocephalus.
Dandy-Walker: the vermis fails to form or stays very small, and the fourth ventricle balloons into a cyst filling an enlarged posterior fossa, often with hydrocephalus.

tricks.label: Count the structures
tricks.text: Chiari I moves one structure down (the tonsils). Chiari II moves two (vermis and medulla) and comes with the open spine.

tricks.label: Which end failed
tricks.text: Anterior neuropore fails, the head end is open: anencephaly. Posterior neuropore fails, the tail end is open: myelomeningocele.

tricks.label: Inside or outside the CNS
tricks.text: Cells that stay inside the brain and cord come from the tube. Cells out in the periphery (ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, melanocytes) come from crest. Microglia are the outsiders from mesoderm.

highYield: High maternal AFP plus high amniotic acetylcholinesterase means an open neural tube defect.
Anencephaly causes polyhydramnios because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid.
Folic acid before conception lowers neural tube defect risk; valproate in pregnancy raises it.
Holoprosencephaly with cyclopia or cleft lip points to trisomy 13 or an SHH defect.
Chiari II almost always comes with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus.
A cape-shaped loss of pain and temperature in an adult with Chiari I means a syrinx.
Schwann cells and adrenal medulla are neural crest; oligodendrocytes and astrocytes are neuroectoderm.
pitfalls: Meningocele has no neural tissue in the sac; myelomeningocele does. Function is usually spared only in meningocele.
Spina bifida occulta does not raise AFP because the defect is covered by skin.
Microglia do not come from neuroectoderm like the other glia; they come from mesoderm.
Dandy-Walker is a missing vermis with a cyst; Chiari II is a vermis that is present but pushed down.

Rhombencephalon splits into metencephalon and myelencephalon
Telencephalon: cerebral hemispheres and lateral ventricles
Diencephalon: thalamus, hypothalamus, retina, third ventricle
Mesencephalon: midbrain and cerebral aqueduct
Metencephalon: pons and cerebellum
Myelencephalon: medulla and lower fourth ventricle

l: Occulta: bony gap only, normal AFP, hair tuft or dimple
Meningocele: meninges and CSF only
Myelomeningocele: cord or roots in the sac, paralysis below the level
Anencephaly: failed anterior neuropore, no skull vault, polyhydramnios
Open defects raise maternal and amniotic AFP

summary: The microscopic parts of neurons, glia, and peripheral nerves, and how each responds to injury. Exam questions tie a cell type to the disease that targets it (Schwann cells in Guillain-Barré, oligodendrocytes in MS and PML) and ask what happens to an axon after it is cut or a neuron after it loses oxygen.

points: Soma: holds the nucleus and Nissl substance (rough ER and ribosomes) for protein synthesis.
Nissl substance fills the soma and dendrites but is absent from the axon hillock and axon.
Dendrites receive input; the axon hillock and initial segment start the action potential; synaptic terminals release transmitter.
Multipolar neurons (one axon, many dendrites): motor neurons and most CNS neurons.
Pseudounipolar neurons: one process that splits into a peripheral and a central branch; found in dorsal root ganglia and most cranial sensory ganglia.
Bipolar neurons: one dendrite and one axon; found in the retina, olfactory epithelium, and the spiral and vestibular ganglia.
Endoneurium: loose connective tissue around each axon and its Schwann cell.
Perineurium: layers of flat epithelioid cells joined by tight junctions around each fascicle; this is the blood-nerve barrier.
Epineurium: dense connective tissue around the whole nerve, carrying its blood vessels.
Surgeons rejoin the perineurium when repairing a cut nerve so fascicles line up.
Schwann cell (PNS, neural crest): myelinates one internode of one axon.
A single Schwann cell can also wrap several unmyelinated axons without making myelin.
Oligodendrocyte (CNS, neuroectoderm): sends processes that myelinate internodes on many axons.
Nodes of Ranvier between internodes hold dense sodium channels, allowing fast saltatory conduction.
Guillain-Barré syndrome: immune attack on Schwann cell myelin, often after Campylobacter jejuni infection.
Multiple sclerosis: autoimmune loss of oligodendrocyte myelin. PML: JC virus kills oligodendrocytes in immunosuppressed patients.
Astrocytes (GFAP positive): foot processes on capillaries support the blood-brain barrier, buffer extracellular potassium, take up glutamate, and form the glial scar after injury.
Microglia: resident CNS macrophages; in HIV encephalitis they form microglial nodules and multinucleated giant cells.
Ependymal cells: ciliated cuboidal to columnar cells lining the ventricles and central canal; modified ependyma of the choroid plexus makes CSF.
Wallerian degeneration: the axon and myelin distal to a cut break down, and macrophages clear the debris.
Central chromatolysis in the cell body: the soma swells, the nucleus moves to the edge, and Nissl substance disperses as the cell ramps up protein synthesis.
PNS regrowth: Schwann cells line up in tubes (bands of Büngner) that guide the regrowing axon at about 1 mm per day.
CNS axons rarely regrow: oligodendrocytes make no guide tubes, CNS myelin contains growth inhibitors, and astrocytes form a glial scar.
Marker of irreversible hypoxic or ischemic neuronal injury, seen about 12 to 24 hours after the insult.
Look: shrunken cell body, intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm, pyknotic nucleus, loss of Nissl substance.
Most vulnerable neurons: hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, cerebellar Purkinje cells, and neocortical pyramidal neurons.
Later stages after an infarct: neutrophils, then macrophages over several days, then reactive gliosis and a cystic space over weeks.

Retina, olfactory epithelium, spiral and vestibular ganglia

Multinucleated giant cells in HIV encephalitis

tricks.label: Endo, peri, epi
tricks.text: Read the layers from inside out: endo around the axon, peri around the fascicle, epi around the whole nerve. Peri is the barrier.

tricks.label: One versus many
tricks.text: Schwann cells are one-to-one (one cell, one internode). Oligodendrocytes are one-to-many (one cell, many axons). So one oligodendrocyte loss strips several axons at once.

tricks.label: Red means dead
tricks.text: A red neuron has bright red cytoplasm and a dark shrunken nucleus. It means irreversible injury from about half a day to a day earlier.

highYield: Nissl substance is missing from the axon hillock, a classic identification point.
Dorsal root ganglion neurons are pseudounipolar; retinal and olfactory neurons are bipolar.
The perineurium, with its tight junctions, forms the blood-nerve barrier.
JC virus in PML destroys oligodendrocytes, so lesions are in white matter.
Microglial nodules with multinucleated giant cells mark HIV encephalitis.
Red neurons appear about 12 to 24 hours after ischemia; CA1 and Purkinje cells die first.
PNS axons regrow along Schwann cell tubes; CNS axons are blocked by the glial scar.
pitfalls: Schwann cells come from neural crest; oligodendrocytes come from the neural tube. Both make myelin.
Wallerian degeneration happens distal to the cut; chromatolysis happens in the cell body proximal to it.
Guillain-Barré targets PNS myelin and spares the CNS; MS targets CNS myelin and spares peripheral nerves.
Choroid plexus epithelium is modified ependyma, so the blood-CSF barrier sits in epithelial tight junctions.

dumps.p: Draw a cross section of a peripheral nerve with two fascicles. Label the three connective tissue layers, a myelinated axon with its Schwann cell, and the blood vessels. Mark which layer is the blood-nerve barrier.

Perineurium around each fascicle
Epineurium around the whole nerve
Perineurium labeled as the blood-nerve barrier with tight junctions
Schwann cell wrapping one internode of one axon
Vessels running in the epineurium

dumps.p: Draw a motor neuron whose axon has been cut. Show what happens in the cell body, the distal axon, and the regrowing tip, and add a short note on why a CNS axon would not regrow.
l: Swollen cell body with nucleus pushed to the edge
Dispersed Nissl substance (central chromatolysis)
Distal axon and myelin breaking down (Wallerian degeneration)
Macrophages clearing debris
Schwann cell tube guiding the new axon
Growth about 1 mm per day
CNS: glial scar, inhibitory myelin, no guide tubes

summary: Where the main cortical areas, basal ganglia, cerebellum, thalamus, brainstem nuclei, and spinal cord regions sit, and what goes wrong when each is damaged. Exam questions give a deficit and ask for the lesion site, or give a lesion and ask for the deficit.

points: Primary motor cortex: precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe; lesion gives contralateral weakness.
Primary somatosensory cortex: postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe; lesion gives contralateral sensory loss.
On both strips the leg sits medially (anterior cerebral artery territory) and the face and arm laterally (middle cerebral artery territory).
Primary visual cortex: banks of the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe; lesion gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
Primary auditory cortex: transverse gyri of the superior temporal gyrus; one-sided lesion causes little hearing loss because each ear projects to both sides.

Broca area (dominant inferior frontal gyrus): lesion gives nonfluent speech with good comprehension. Wernicke area (dominant posterior superior temporal gyrus): fluent speech that makes no sense, with poor comprehension.
Direct pathway: striatum inhibits the internal globus pallidus (GPi), releasing the thalamus, so movement increases.
Indirect pathway: striatum inhibits the external globus pallidus, releasing the subthalamic nucleus, which drives GPi to inhibit the thalamus, so movement decreases.
Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta excites the direct pathway through D1 and inhibits the indirect pathway through D2; both effects increase movement.
Parkinson disease: loss of nigral dopamine neurons (Lewy bodies with alpha-synuclein) leaves the indirect pathway dominant, giving too little movement.
Huntington disease: early loss of GABA neurons in the caudate (indirect pathway) leaves the thalamus released, giving chorea; CAG repeat in HTT on chromosome 4.
Subthalamic nucleus lesion (often a small stroke): contralateral hemiballismus.
Compares the intended movement with what actually happens and corrects timing and force.
Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex and are inhibitory (GABA) onto the deep nuclei.
Vermis (midline) lesion: truncal ataxia and a wide-based gait; alcohol damages the anterior vermis.
Hemisphere lesion: ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and falling toward the lesion side.
Signs are ipsilateral because cerebellar output crosses to the opposite cortex, and the corticospinal tract crosses back.
Relay station: almost all sensation except smell passes through it to the cortex.
Thalamic infarct: contralateral loss of all body sensation.
Weeks to months later some patients develop thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy): burning contralateral pain set off by light touch.
Cranial nerve nuclei: midbrain III and IV; pons V, VI, VII, VIII; medulla IX, X, XII; the XI nucleus sits in the upper cervical cord.
Gray horns: dorsal horn sensory, ventral horn motor (alpha and gamma motor neurons), lateral horn T1 to L2 sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
White columns: dorsal (fasciculus gracilis for legs, cuneatus for arms), lateral (lateral corticospinal tract), and anterolateral (spinothalamic tract).
Enlargements: cervical (about C4 to T1) for the arm plexus and lumbosacral (about L2 to S3) for the leg plexus.
The cord ends as the conus medullaris near L1 to L2 in adults; roots below form the cauda equina.
Arousal needs the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) of the upper pons and midbrain, projecting through the thalamus to both hemispheres.
Coma comes from ARAS damage or from dysfunction of both hemispheres; one damaged hemisphere alone does not cause coma.
Delirium: acute, fluctuating loss of attention, often from infection, drugs, or metabolic upset, and usually reversible.
Brain death: irreversible loss of all brain and brainstem function: coma, no brainstem reflexes, and apnea with a high PaCO2; spinal reflexes may remain.

rows: Contralateral weakness with upper motor neuron signs
Contralateral loss of touch and position sense
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often macular sparing

Nonfluent aphasia, comprehension intact, poor repetition
Fluent aphasia, poor comprehension, poor repetition

tricks.label: Medial for Music, Lateral for Light
tricks.text: MGN relays hearing; LGN relays vision.

tricks.label: TRAP
tricks.text: Parkinson disease: Tremor at rest, Rigidity (cogwheel), Akinesia or bradykinesia, Postural instability.

tricks.label: Don't Eat Greasy Foods
tricks.text: Deep cerebellar nuclei from lateral to medial: Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial.

tricks.label: Dopamine always says go
tricks.text: Through D1 it pushes the go pathway; through D2 it blocks the stop pathway. Lose dopamine and you lose movement.

highYield: Leg weakness greater than arm weakness points to the medial motor strip (anterior cerebral artery).
Huntington disease: caudate atrophy with enlarged lateral ventricles, autosomal dominant, anticipation.
Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral signs; most other cerebral lesions cause contralateral signs.
The conus ends near L1 to L2, so a lumbar puncture lower down misses the cord.
A thalamic stroke can cause contralateral burning pain weeks later (thalamic pain syndrome).
Coma needs ARAS damage or bilateral hemisphere dysfunction.
Brain death keeps spinal reflexes but loses every brainstem reflex and the drive to breathe.
pitfalls: Broca and Wernicke aphasia both impair repetition; tell them apart by fluency and comprehension.
Parkinson disease is too little movement from a stronger indirect pathway; Huntington disease is too much movement from a weaker indirect pathway.
A vermis lesion affects the trunk on both sides; a hemisphere lesion affects the limbs on one side.
VPL carries the body and VPM carries the face; M for mouth helps place taste in VPM.
Delirium fluctuates and the patient can be roused; coma does not fluctuate and the patient cannot be roused.

dumps.p: Draw the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways from cortex to thalamus. Mark each connection as excitatory or inhibitory, add the substantia nigra with D1 and D2, and show what changes in Parkinson and Huntington disease.

Direct: striatum inhibits GPi, thalamus released
Indirect: striatum inhibits GPe, subthalamic nucleus released, GPi driven
GPi inhibits the thalamus
Dopamine excites direct via D1, inhibits indirect via D2
Parkinson: nigral dopamine loss, less movement
Huntington: caudate indirect neuron loss, chorea
Subthalamic lesion: hemiballismus

Postcentral: contralateral sensory loss

Broca: nonfluent aphasia, comprehension intact
Wernicke: fluent aphasia, poor comprehension

summary: The meninges and the spaces between them, the dural folds that set up herniation, the CSF spaces used for lumbar puncture, the blood-brain barrier, and CSF findings in meningitis. Exam questions place a bleed in the right space, predict what a herniation compresses, and read a CSF panel.

points: Dura mater: tough outer layer; in the skull its two layers split to hold the dural venous sinuses.
Arachnoid: thin, avascular, pressed against the dura; pia: clings to the brain surface and follows every sulcus.
Epidural space: potential space in the skull, real space in the spinal canal (fat and veins).
Subdural space: potential space between dura and arachnoid. Subarachnoid space: real space with CSF and the large cerebral arteries.
Epidural hematoma: a skull fracture at the pterion tears the middle meningeal artery; lens-shaped clot that stops at sutures; lucid interval, then rapid decline.
Subdural hematoma: torn bridging veins between cortex and dural sinuses; crescent clot that crosses sutures; elderly, alcohol use, infant shaking.

Spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage: usually a ruptured berry aneurysm (most often anterior communicating artery); sudden worst headache of life; xanthochromic CSF; vasospasm about 3 to 10 days later.
Falx cerebri divides the hemispheres; tentorium cerebelli separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum, with the midbrain in its notch.
Subfalcine herniation: cingulate gyrus slides under the falx and compresses the anterior cerebral artery, causing contralateral leg weakness.

Uncal herniation: medial temporal lobe slides through the tentorial notch and presses on CN III (dilated, fixed pupil first, then down and out eye), the posterior cerebral artery (contralateral hemianopia), and the cerebral peduncle.
Compressing the ipsilateral peduncle gives contralateral weakness; pushing the opposite peduncle against the tentorium (Kernohan notch) gives ipsilateral weakness.
Tonsillar herniation: cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum compress the medulla, stopping breathing and circulation.

notes.h: Cisterns, CSF flow, and lumbar puncture
points: Cisterns are wide parts of the subarachnoid space, such as the cisterna magna behind the medulla.
Choroid plexus makes about 500 mL of CSF a day; about 150 mL is present at any time.
Flow: lateral ventricles, foramina of Monro, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, foramina of Luschka and Magendie, subarachnoid space.
Arachnoid granulations return CSF to the superior sagittal sinus.
The lumbar cistern runs from the conus (L1 to L2) to S2 and holds the cauda equina; puncture at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5, using the iliac crest line (about L4).
Needle path: skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura, arachnoid, subarachnoid space.
Blood-brain barrier: endothelial tight junctions with no fenestrations, a basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes.
Lipid-soluble molecules cross freely; glucose (GLUT1) and amino acids need carriers. L-dopa crosses; dopamine does not.
Blood-CSF barrier: choroid plexus capillaries are leaky, so the barrier is the tight junctions of the choroid epithelium.
Circumventricular organs have no barrier so they can sample or secrete into blood: area postrema (vomiting), posterior pituitary, OVLT, subfornical organ, median eminence.
Normal: opening pressure about 6 to 20 cm H2O, 0 to 5 lymphocytes per µL, protein 15 to 45 mg/dL, glucose about 60% of blood glucose (40 to 70 mg/dL).
Low glucose means organisms or inflammatory cells are using it: bacterial, fungal, or tuberculous meningitis.
Neutrophils point to bacteria; lymphocytes point to viral, fungal, or tuberculous causes.
Guillain-Barré: high protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation).

charts.title: Intracranial bleeds
rows: Temporal blow, lucid interval, rapid decline
Older adult or heavy drinker, slow confusion

charts.title: Herniation syndromes
rows: CN III, posterior cerebral artery, cerebral peduncle
Cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum

tricks.label: Artery is fast, vein is slow
tricks.text: Epidural bleeds are arterial and expand in hours. Subdural bleeds are venous and can build over days to weeks.

tricks.label: Viral leaves the sugar alone
tricks.text: Of the four meningitis types, only viral meningitis keeps CSF glucose normal.

tricks.label: Barrier-free zones do a job
tricks.text: Each circumventricular organ needs blood contact for a reason: the area postrema tastes toxins, the OVLT reads osmolality, the posterior pituitary releases hormones.

highYield: Pterion fracture plus lucid interval means an epidural hematoma from the middle meningeal artery.
A blown pupil on one side is the earliest sign of uncal herniation (CN III compression).
Rising intracranial pressure can produce the Cushing triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing.
Lumbar puncture is done below the conus at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5.
Arachnoid granulations drain CSF into the superior sagittal sinus.
The area postrema lacks a barrier, so blood-borne toxins can trigger vomiting.
High protein with a normal cell count in CSF means Guillain-Barré syndrome.
pitfalls: Epidural clots stop at sutures; subdural clots cross sutures but stop at the falx and tentorium.
Uncal herniation usually gives contralateral weakness, but a Kernohan notch gives ipsilateral weakness and can mislead about the side.
Very early viral meningitis can show neutrophils; glucose stays normal, which keeps it apart from bacterial meningitis.
Choroid plexus capillaries are leaky; the blood-CSF barrier is in the epithelium, not the endothelium.

Superior sagittal sinus between dural layers
Bridging vein crossing the subdural space
Arachnoid granulation projecting into the sinus
Epidural bleed between skull and dura (artery)
Subdural bleed between dura and arachnoid (vein)
Subarachnoid bleed in the CSF space (aneurysm)

dumps.p: Build a table comparing CSF in bacterial, viral, fungal, and tuberculous meningitis and Guillain-Barré syndrome. Include opening pressure, cell type, protein, and glucose, and add normal values in the top row.

Bacterial: neutrophils, high protein, low glucose
Viral: lymphocytes, normal glucose

summary: The receptors that pick up touch, pain, and stretch, the two main sensory tracts and where they cross, spinal reflexes, referred pain, how the body turns pain down, and the three common headache types. Exam questions ask you to predict sensory loss from a cord lesion and to name the root of a reflex.

points: Fast-adapting receptors signal change (Meissner, Pacinian); slow-adapting receptors signal steady pressure or stretch (Merkel, Ruffini).
Free nerve endings carry pain and temperature over thin Aδ fibers (sharp pain, cold) and unmyelinated C fibers (burning pain, warmth).
Muscle spindles lie parallel to muscle fibers and sense length and its rate of change (Ia and II afferents); gamma motor neurons keep them taut.
Golgi tendon organs lie in series at the muscle-tendon junction and sense tension (Ib afferents).
Dorsal column medial lemniscus (fine touch, vibration, position): first neuron ascends on the same side in the dorsal column.
It synapses in nucleus gracilis or cuneatus in the lower medulla, crosses as internal arcuate fibers, rises as the medial lemniscus to VPL, then to the postcentral gyrus.
Spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature, crude touch): first neuron synapses in the dorsal horn, and the second neuron crosses within one or two segments in the anterior white commissure.
It rises in the contralateral anterolateral cord to VPL, then to the postcentral gyrus.
Cord lesion on one side: same-side loss of vibration and position below, opposite-side loss of pain and temperature starting one or two segments below.
Lesion above the lower medulla: all sensory loss is contralateral because both tracts have crossed.
Brown-Séquard hemisection: ipsilateral weakness (corticospinal), ipsilateral loss of vibration and position (dorsal column), contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic).
At the lesion level: ipsilateral loss of all sensation and lower motor neuron signs; a lesion above T1 can add an ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
Syringomyelia: a fluid cavity in the central cervical cord cuts the crossing spinothalamic fibers on both sides.
Result: bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders and arms, with touch preserved; a growing syrinx adds hand muscle wasting.
Stretch reflex: tendon tap stretches the spindle, Ia afferent synapses directly on the alpha motor neuron, the same muscle contracts (monosynaptic).
An Ia inhibitory interneuron relaxes the antagonist at the same time (reciprocal inhibition).
Golgi tendon organ reflex: high tension fires Ib afferents, which act through an inhibitory interneuron to relax the same muscle.
Withdrawal reflex: a painful stimulus flexes the injured limb through several interneurons; the crossed extensor reflex stiffens the opposite limb to bear weight.
Reflex roots: biceps C5, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1.
Visceral and skin afferents from the same spinal segment converge on the same dorsal horn neurons, so the brain blames the skin.
Heart (T1 to T4): pain felt in the chest, left arm, and jaw.
Diaphragm (phrenic nerve C3 to C5): pain felt at the shoulder tip.
Gate control: touch fibers (Aβ) activate inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn that damp pain transmission; rubbing an injury helps.
Descending control: the periaqueductal gray drives the rostral medulla (serotonin) and locus coeruleus (norepinephrine) to inhibit dorsal horn pain neurons.
Endogenous opioids (enkephalins, endorphins, dynorphins) cut transmitter release presynaptically and hyperpolarize the postsynaptic neuron.
Neuropathic pain comes from damage to the nervous system itself: postherpetic neuralgia, phantom limb pain, thalamic pain syndrome.
Migraine: often unilateral, pulsating, 4 to 72 hours, with nausea and light sensitivity; trigeminovascular activation releases CGRP; aura comes from cortical spreading depression.
Cluster headache: severe periorbital pain for 15 to 180 minutes with same-side tearing, runny nose, and sometimes ptosis and miosis; more common in men.
Tension headache: bilateral band-like pressure, no nausea, not worse with activity.

tricks.text: Achilles S1 to S2, patellar L3 to L4, biceps C5 to C6, triceps C7 to C8.

tricks.label: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive
tricks.text: The phrenic nerve comes from C3 to C5, so diaphragm irritation is felt at the shoulder tip (C3 to C5 dermatomes).

tricks.label: Pain crosses at once, touch crosses late
tricks.text: Spinothalamic fibers cross within a segment or two of entering the cord; dorsal column fibers wait until the medulla. That is why a hemisection splits the losses to opposite sides.

highYield: Brown-Séquard: same-side weakness and vibration loss, opposite-side pain and temperature loss.
Syringomyelia: cape-like pain and temperature loss with touch spared, often with Chiari I.
The stretch reflex is the only monosynaptic reflex; the Golgi tendon organ reflex relaxes the muscle.
Pacinian corpuscles sense vibration and adapt fast; Merkel discs sense steady pressure and adapt slowly.
Shoulder tip pain can come from the diaphragm (C3 to C5).
The periaqueductal gray drives descending opioid pain control.
Cluster headache gives same-side tearing and runny nose; migraine gives nausea and light sensitivity.
pitfalls: Muscle spindles are in parallel and sense length; Golgi tendon organs are in series and sense tension.
A dorsal column lesion causes loss on the same side; a spinothalamic lesion causes loss on the opposite side.
Syringomyelia loses pain and temperature on both sides; Brown-Séquard loses them on one side.
Postherpetic neuralgia is pain that lasts months after the shingles rash heals; it is neuropathic pain from nerve damage the virus left behind, not ongoing infection.
Migraine is worse with activity and makes patients lie still; cluster headache makes patients pace.

summary: How vision, hearing, balance, taste, and smell are sensed and carried to the brain, plus the glands of the eye. Exam questions ask you to predict a visual field defect, read a pupil exam, interpret Weber and Rinne tests, and explain phototransduction and night blindness.

points: Each retina's nasal half sees the temporal field; nasal fibers cross at the optic chiasm.
So each optic tract carries the opposite visual field to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN).
Optic radiations: the Meyer loop runs through the temporal lobe carrying the upper field; the parietal radiations carry the lower field.
Both end on the banks of the calcarine sulcus; the macula is at the occipital pole, which has a dual blood supply.
Light reflex: CN II to the pretectal nucleus, then both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, CN III, ciliary ganglion, and the pupillary sphincter; both pupils constrict.
Near response: convergence, pupil constriction, and a rounder lens (ciliary muscle contracts, zonules relax).
Relative afferent pupillary defect: light in the damaged eye constricts both pupils less, so both dilate when the light swings to it; pupils are equal at rest.
Anisocoria from disease is an efferent problem: a large pupil from CN III palsy, a small one from Horner syndrome. A small difference can also be a harmless normal variant.
Compressive CN III lesions (aneurysm, uncal herniation) hit the outer pupillary fibers first; diabetic CN III palsy usually spares the pupil.
Argyll Robertson pupil (neurosyphilis): small, irregular pupils that constrict to near focus but not to light.
In the dark, high cGMP holds cGMP-gated sodium channels open, so the rod stays depolarized and releases glutamate steadily.
Light converts 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal in rhodopsin, which activates transducin.
Transducin activates phosphodiesterase, cGMP falls, the channels close, and the cell hyperpolarizes, cutting glutamate release.
Retinal comes from vitamin A, so deficiency hits rods first: night blindness, then dry eye, Bitot spots, and corneal damage.
Rods: periphery, dim light, one pigment. Cones: fovea, color (three opsins), sharp detail.
Ciliary body epithelium secretes aqueous humor into the posterior chamber; it flows through the pupil to the anterior chamber.
It drains at the iridocorneal angle through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm; blocked outflow raises pressure (glaucoma).
Tear film: outer lipid layer (meibomian glands), middle watery layer (lacrimal gland), inner mucin layer (conjunctival goblet cells).
Lacrimal gland parasympathetics: CN VII, greater petrosal nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion, then to the gland.
Sound moves the tympanic membrane, malleus, incus, and stapes, which pushes the oval window; the size difference and lever action raise pressure about 20 times.
Endolymph in the scala media is potassium rich; when stereocilia bend, potassium flows in and depolarizes the hair cell.
Tonotopy: the narrow, stiff base hears high pitch; the wide, floppy apex hears low pitch. Noise and age damage the base first.
Weber and Rinne separate conductive loss (outer or middle ear) from sensorineural loss (cochlea or CN VIII).
Semicircular canals sense angular acceleration as endolymph lags and bends the cupula.
Utricle (horizontal) and saccule (vertical) sense linear acceleration and gravity through otoliths.
Vestibulo-ocular reflex: turning the head moves the eyes the same amount the other way to keep the image steady.
One-sided vestibular loss unbalances the input, causing vertigo and nystagmus with the fast phase away from the bad side.
Motion sickness comes from conflict between vestibular, visual, and body position signals.
Taste: anterior two thirds via CN VII (chorda tympani), posterior third via CN IX, to the nucleus solitarius, then VPM, then the gustatory cortex.
Smell: olfactory receptor neurons send axons through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, then to olfactory cortex with no thalamic relay.
Cribriform plate fracture tears these axons, causing anosmia and sometimes CSF leaking from the nose.

tricks.label: COWS
tricks.text: Cold Opposite, Warm Same: caloric testing, the fast phase of nystagmus beats away from a cold ear and toward a warm ear.

tricks.label: Pie in the sky, pie on the floor
tricks.text: Temporal (Meyer loop) lesions take the upper quarter of the field; parietal lesions take the lower quarter.

tricks.label: Weber picks a side
tricks.text: In conductive loss the sound goes to the bad ear. In sensorineural loss it goes to the good ear.

tricks.label: Light turns rods off
tricks.text: Rods and cones are most active in the dark and hyperpolarize when light hits them.

highYield: Bitemporal hemianopia means the chiasm, most often a pituitary adenoma.
PCA stroke spares the macula; an optic tract lesion does not.
Argyll Robertson pupils accommodate but do not react to light, classic for neurosyphilis.
Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness because rods need 11-cis retinal.
Endolymph is potassium rich; potassium entry depolarizes hair cells.
High-frequency hearing loss with age or noise reflects damage at the cochlear base.
Smell is the only sense that reaches cortex without a thalamic relay; cribriform fracture causes anosmia.
CN VII damage proximal to the greater petrosal branch causes a dry eye.
pitfalls: A relative afferent pupillary defect does not cause anisocoria; unequal pupils point to an efferent lesion.
In a negative Rinne (bone better than air), the loss is conductive.
Semicircular canals sense turning; utricle and saccule sense straight-line motion and tilt.
Taste from the anterior tongue travels with CN VII, while touch from the same area travels with CN V3.
Light hyperpolarizes rods by closing sodium channels; it does not open them.
